name: Zapoteco Central de Ocotlán de Morelos, San Antonino variety
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 8 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Olson, Donald & Anne Blackman de Olson. 1982. Cómo leer y escribir el zapoteco [colophon: Idioma: Zapoteco Central de Ocotlán de Morelos]. 1a ed. México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano, A.C. 33 pp. ISBN 968-31-0138-0. SIL Mexico archive entry 12160 (SIL REAP scan); duplicate copy Colmex hdl 20.500.11986/COLMEX/10049258.
catalog_locator: Lección 2 §4 'El acento', p. 4 = SIL scan p. 8; Lección 12 §2 'El tono', p. 26 = SIL scan p. 30
catalog_quote: El acento. El acento escrito sobre una vocal indica que esa sílaba se pronuncia con más intensidad. En el zapoteco ocupamos las mismas reglas que en el español. Sin embargo, el resultado es diferente. La vocal acentuada es larga, como en dumí y laní. Palabras que no tienen acento escrito siguen las mismas reglas que en el español, como en lari y begu. La primera vocal en cada palabra es larga. En los ejemplos: dumí y laní, la segunda vocal es larga. [p. 26] El tono. Un fenómeno en muchas lenguas del mundo es el que las palabras tienen tonos. En el zapoteco hay tres tonos: bajo, alto, y acendente. Estos tonos no se escriben, porque los que hablan zapoteco ya saben qué tonos tiene cada palabra. Son pocos los casos en los que dos palabras se escriben igual pero tienen tonos diferentes; vea los siguientes ejemplos.

new_statements.translation: The accent. A written accent on a vowel indicates that that syllable is pronounced with more intensity. In Zapotec we use the same rules as in Spanish. However, the result is different. The accented vowel is long, as in dumí ['money'] and laní ['fiesta']. Words that have no written accent follow the same rules as in Spanish, as in lari ['clothes'] and begu ['comb']. The first vowel in each word is long. In the examples dumí and laní, the second vowel is long. [p. 26:] In Zapotec there are three tones: low, high and rising. These tones are not written, because Zapotec speakers already know which tones each word has.

Sin embargo, el resultado es diferente. La vocal acentuada es larga, como en dumí y laní. Palabras que no tienen acento escrito siguen las mismas reglas que en el español, como en lari y begu. La primera vocal en cada palabra es larga. En los ejemplos: dumí y laní, la segunda vocal es larga."). p. 30 = printed p. 26, item "2. El tono": "En el zapoteco hay tres tonos: bajo, alto, y acendente…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ocotlán Zapotec has three lexical tones (low, high, rising) and, separately, a word-level accent (greater intensity plus vowel length). Its placement is described only by analogy with Spanish orthography: words without a written accent take the Spanish default, which for these vowel-final disyllables is the first (penultimate) syllable (lari, begu); words with a written accent are stressed on the final syllable (dumí, laní). So the default is penultimate with lexically specified final-stress words, which the orthography marks; stress is therefore not fully predictable from the word shape (lari vs laní).
new_statements.exceptions: Words carrying a written accent are stressed on the final syllable (dumí, laní; the dictionary draft §2.3 likewise speaks of words 'con la última sílaba acentuada', e.g. nipi 'pulque', llili 'algodón' with final stress). The 2009 alphabet notes and the dictionary §0.2 add only that accented plain vowels are longer than others.
new_statements.domain_note: Pedagogical literacy primer, not a phonological analysis; the statement concerns the orthographic accent and its phonetic correlates (intensity, length) on isolated words in the primer's word lists; nothing on phrase-level stress or on how stress interacts with the three tones. The dictionary draft's §0.2 (Olson & Olson c. 1980) and the 2009 alphabet notes repeat only the length correlate and the 'each syllable has its own tone' remark.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted primer is labelled 'Zapoteco Central de Ocotlán de Morelos' and was produced by Donald and Anne Olson (SIL), whose Ocotlán fieldwork was in San Antonino Ocotlán (= San Antonino Castillo Velasco; cf. their 1956 booklet 'Dialecto de San Antonino, Oax.' and the 1970 Tlalocan texts recorded there). SIL files all these materials under Ocotlán Zapotec [zac] = Western Ocotlán Zapotec = ocot1244, so the statement is for the language-level entry; note that the same ISO code also covers Santiago Apóstol (Padilla Pérez 2010; Merrill's 2005 numbers booklet) and other Ocotlán-district towns (Santa Ana Zegache, Santa Lucía/Asunción Ocotlán surveys), for which no separate glottocodes exist.

sources.note: Lección 2 §4 'El acento' (printed p. 4 = p. 8): the written accent marks the syllable pronounced with more intensity; Zapotec uses the same accent rules as Spanish; unmarked words (lari 'ropa', begu 'peine') are stressed on the first vowel, marked words (dumí 'dinero', laní 'fiesta') on the second; the stressed vowel is long. Lección 12 §2 'El tono' (p. 26 = p. 30): three tones (bajo, alto, ascendente), not.

sources.note: Sección I §0.2 'Aclaraciones' (p. 1): 'Las vocales sencillas que llevan el acento tienen un sonido más largo que las otras: dumí dinero, laní fiesta. En zapoteco cada sílaba tiene su propio tono, pero éste no se indica en forma escrita.' No positional rule; grammar sketch §2.3 (pp. 10-11) treats morphophonemics of words 'con la última sílaba acentuada', i.e. some words carry lexical final stress.
